extracted.intended_audience: classicists, historians of mathematics, translators and mathematicians studying Archimedes' Greek terminology
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and explain Archimedean/Greek technical terminology for plane and solid geometry (names, verbs, phraseology) as used in translations and scholarly work. Emphasises how Archimedes (and related authors) use particular words and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gnomon terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: A gnomon is γνώμων, and its breadth (πλάτος) is the breadth of each end; a gnomon of breadth equal to BI, γνώμων πλάτος ἔχων ἴσον τῷ BI; (a gnomon) whose breadth is greater by one segment than the breadth of the gnomon last taken away οὗ πλάτος ἑνὶ τμάματι μεῖζον τοῦ πλάτεος τοῦ προσαυτοῦ ἀφαιρουμένου γνωμονος.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains literal Greek phrasing used to describe gnomons and comparative constructions (e.g. 'greater by one segment'); useful when translating comparative descriptions of successive gnomons or constructing equalities involving gnomon breadths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygon vocabulary and qualifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: A polygon is πολύγωνον; an equilateral polygon is ἰσόπλευρον; a polygon of an even number of sides or angles ἀρτιόπλευρον or ἀρτιόγωνον; a polygon with all its sides equal except BA, ἴσας ἔχοντας πλευρὰς χωρὶς τῶν BAA; a polygon with its sides, excluding the base, equal and even in number τὰς πλευρὰς ἔχον χωρὶς τῆς βάσεως ἴσας καὶ ἀρτίους; an equilateral polygon the number of whose sides is measured by four ... πολύγωνον ἰσόπλευρον, οὗ αἱ πλευραὶ ὑπὸ τετράδος μετροῦνται; a chiliagon χιλιάγωνον.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives Greek terms and idioms for common polygon properties (equilateral, even-sided, exceptions like 'all equal except one side'), and the phrasing used to state the number of sides is measured by some number (e.g. 'measured by four'). Important for accurate rendering of qualifiers and counting phrases in translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straight lines subtending polygon sides (technical phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The straight lines subtending two sides of the polygon (i.e. joining angles next but one to each other) are described as αἱ ὑποτείνουσαι (or ὑποτείνουσαι τὰς μιᾷ ἐλάσσονας τῶν ἡμίσεων for the straight line subtending one less than half the number of sides n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records the Greek technical phrase for diagonals or lines 'subtending' non-adjacent vertices and the special phrase when the subtended number relates to half the sides. Useful for translating combinatorial/positional descriptions in polygon propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle and circumference terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: A circle is κύκλος; the centre is κέντρον, the circumference περιφέρεια (used both for whole circumference and for an arc), and sometimes περίμετρος appears (as in Archimedes' Sand-reckoner for 'perimeter').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that περιφέρεια commonly denotes arc or whole circumference and that περίμετρος appears rarely; relevant for choosing correct English term (arc vs. circumference vs. perimeter) depending on context in Archimedean usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radius and diameter phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: The radius is ἡ ἐκ τοῦ κέντρου (used without article as a predicate); a diameter is διάμετρος, and the circle on AE as diameter is ὁ περὶ διάμετρον τὴν AE κύκλος.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows typical Greek constructions for stating 'a radius of the circle' and 'circle described on AE as diameter'—important when rendering predicative uses and expressions 'the circle whose radius is X'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chord, segment, semicircle and sector expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Chord: no specialized single word; phrases like εὐθεῖα ἐμπεσοῦσα or simply ἐν τῷ κύκλῳ (εὐθεῖα). Segment of a circle τμῆμα κύκλου (or plane segment τμῆμα ἐπίπεδον). Semicircle ἡμικύκλιον; sector τομεύς or ἐπίπεδος τομεὺς κύκλου (to distinguish from solid sector στερεός τομεύς).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives preferred Greek phrases for chords and for distinguishing plane sector vs. solid sector; indicates how sector sides (radii) are called πλευρά and how sectors equal/similar are expressed. Use these when translating constructions and equality statements about sectors and segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribed and circumscribed polygon phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: To inscribe in or circumscribe about a circle: ἐγγράφειν (εἰς or ἐν) and περιγράφειν (περί with acc.); περιγεγραμμένος used with dative. A polygon inscribed in a segment is ἐπὶ τῆς ... πολύγωνον ἐγγεγράφθω εἰς τὸ ... τμῆμα. Regular polygon 'inscribed in a sector' and 'circumscribed about a sector' have specific Greek constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records the verbs and case patterns used for inscription/circumscription and the special phrasing for polygons relative to sectors and segments; helpful to render active/passive imperatives and participles in English translations of constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary for leftover areas between polygon and circle
rubrics_metrics.description: When a polygon is inscribed in a circle, the segments left over between the sides of the polygon and the subtended arcs are περιλειπόμενα τμήματα; when circumscribed, the spaces are τὰ περιλειπόμενα τῆς περιγραφῆς τμήματα, τὰ περιλειπόμενα σχήματα, τὰ περιλείμματα or τὰ ἀπολείμματα.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives several synonymous Greek terms for the 'remainders' or 'leftover' parts when approximating circle by polygons, useful for accurate translation of limiting/progressive approximation arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere and spherical terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Sphere σφαῖρα; centre κέντρον, radius ἡ ἐκ τοῦ κέντρου, diameter διάμετρος. Segments τμήματα σφαίρας or τμήματα σφαιρικά; hemisphere ἡμισφαίριον; curved surface ἐπιφάνεια; base (βάσις), vertex (κορυφή), height (ὕψος) used for segments of a sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translates geometric vocabulary for spheres and their parts and records adjectival forms (spherical segments) and usage for 'curved surface' (ἐπιφάνεια), supporting consistent rendering of 3D terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid sector and related terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid sector (τομεὺς στερεός) is the figure bounded by a cone with its vertex at the centre of a sphere and the part of the surface of the sphere within the cone; the segment of the sphere included in the sector is τὸ τμῆμα τῆς σφαίρας τὸ ἐν τῷ τομεῖ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes plane sector (τομεύς) from solid sector (τομεὺς στερεός) and gives the precise Greek phrasing for the solid-sector construction—important when translating Archimedean volume/surface propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism and pyramid terminology and phrasing for 'describing on a base'
rubrics_metrics.description: A prism is πρῖσμα, a pyramid is πυραμίς. ἀναγράφειν ἀπὸ is used of describing a prism or pyramid 'on' a rectilineal figure as base (e.g., ἀναγεγράφθω ἀπὸ τοῦ εὐθυγράμμου πρῖσμα). Surface (ἐπιφάνεια) phrasing often excludes the base by qualification (ἡ ἐπιφάνεια τοῦ πρίσματος ἡ ἐκ τῶν παραλληλογράμμων συγκειμένη).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the verbs and syntactic constructions used when forming solids from bases, the naming of surfaces excluding bases, and how bounding faces/triangles are expressed—useful for translations of solid constructions and surface statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cone terminology and special forms (isosceles/right/oblique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclidean Elements introduce right cones; Archimedes generally describes a right cone as κῶνος ἰσοσκελής (isosceles cone), sometimes ὀρθός (right). Vertex κορυφή, base βάσις, axis ἄξων, height ὕψος; generator is called a side (πλευρά). Frustum described as 'surface of the cone between the parallel planes' rather than a special word; segment of a cone ἀπότμαμα κώνου used for portion cut off towards the vertex by a plane making an elliptic section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how Archimedes and predecessors name types of cones and how frusta and cone-segments are referred to without a unique word; gives wording for axis-of-segment and enveloping cone concepts—important for consistent translation of cone-based solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solid rhombus (ῥόμβος στερεός) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid rhombus is the figure made up of two cones having their base common, their vertices on opposite sides of it, and their axes in one straight line (ῥόμβος στερεός).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives Greek phrasing and composition (two cones with common base) for the solid rhombus; helpful when encountering this less common solid in translations or commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cylinder vocabulary and phrasing for parts and frusta
rubrics_metrics.description: Right cylinder κύλινδρος ὀρθός; base βάσις (one base ἡ ἑτέρα βάσις), axis ἄξων, height ὕψος, generator πλευρά. Cylindrical surface between two generators ἡ ἀποτεμνομένη κυλινδρικὴ ἐπιφάνεια ὑπὸ τῶν AT, ΒΔ. Frustum of a cylinder τοπος κυλίνδρου (portion intercepted between two parallel sections which are elliptic and not circular); axis of frustum joins centres of sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records Greek terms for cylinder parts, for the partial surface between generators, and phrasing for frusta (including phrase identifying axis as joining centres).

rubrics_metrics.name: General conic-section terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Conic elements: κωνικὰ στοιχεῖα, τὰ κωνικά (the theory of conics). Any conic section κώνου τομή ὁποιαοῦν. Chords εὐθείαι ἐν τῇ τοῦ κώνου τομῃ ἀγμέναι. Archimedes uses διάμετρος for diameters (axes) of complete conics and ἐπιψαύουσα/ἐφαπτομένη for tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lays out the general vocabulary for conics and notes Archimedes' tendency to call axes 'diameters' and his tangent words; useful for interpreting axis/diameter terminology that differs from modern usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parabola-specific terms and usages
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the axis of a complete parabola is called a diameter; other diameters are lines parallel to the diameter. A segment of a parabola is τμῆμα (bounded by a straight line and the section); Archimedes defines the diameter of any segment as the line bisecting all the straight lines (chords) drawn parallel to its base. Frustum (τόμος) has lesser and greater base (ἐλάσσων and μείζων βάσις). 'Latus rectum' is phrased as the line double of the line drawn as far as the axis (διπλασία τᾶς μέχρι τοῦ ἄξονος). 'Parameter' phrasing parallels Apollonius: the rectangle applied to a line equal to the square of the ordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives Archimedean constructions and technical definitions for parabola segments, diameters, frusta, and analytic notions (latus rectum/parameter/ordinates) with the precise Greek expressions used; essential for rendering analytic descriptions in geometrical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbola terminology (asymptotes and centre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymptotes described as the lines approaching nearest to the section of the obtuse-angled cone (αἔγγιστα τᾶς τοῦ ἀμβλυγωνίου κώνου τομάς). Archimedes does not describe the centre as such but calls the centre the point at which the lines nearest meet (τὸ σημεῖον, καθ᾽ ὃ αἱ ἔγγιστα συμπίπτουσιν).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies Archimedes' phrasing for asymptotes and centre-like notions in hyperbolic contexts—helpful when mapping classical descriptions to modern analytic vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipse terminology (axes, conjugate axis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Major and minor axes are μείζων and ἐλάσσων διάμετρος; 'the rectangle contained by the diameters' τὸ περιεχόμενον ὑπὸ τῶν διαμέτρων. One axis is conjugate (συζυγής) to the other; centre κέντρον.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the Greek words for axes and the term for conjugate axes, plus the standard phrasing for rectangles formed by diameters—useful for translating area relations and axis-based constructions in elliptic propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conoids and spheroids: genesis and naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Conoid (κωνοειδές) and spheroid (σφαιροειδές) are derived terms meaning 'resembling' cone or sphere; right-angled conoid (ὀρθογώνιον) and obtuse-angled (ἀμβλυγώνιον) qualifiers are transferred from conics. A spheroid may be oblong (παραμακὴς σφαιροειδές) or flat (ἐπιπλατύ σφαιροειδές) depending on axis of revolution. Vertex κορυφή, axis defined as diameter which remained fixed, segment and base defined as for cones/spheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how Archimedes describes solids of revolution and his terminology choices; records special conventions (e.g. axis/direction, enveloping cone for hyperboloid) important for interpreting 3D constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axis and segment definitions for various solids
rubrics_metrics.description: The axis (ἄξων) of a segment is defined differently: (a) paraboloid: straight line cut off within the segment from the line drawn through the vertex of the segment parallel to the axis of the conoid; (b) hyperboloid: straight line cut off within the segment from the line drawn through the vertex of the segment and the vertex of the cone enveloping the conoid; (c) spheroid: part cut off from the straight line joining the vertices of the two segments into which the base divides the spheroid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives case-by-case rules for what counts as the 'axis' of a segment of different solids—critical for correct interpretation of Archimedean arguments that refer to 'the axis' of a piece of solid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiral construction and associated vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: Spiral (ἕλιξ) constructed by a straight line in a plane turning uniformly about one extremity while a point moves uniformly along the line starting from the fixed extremity; distances along the line are εὐθεῖαι διανυσθεῖσαι, times are ὁ χρόνοι. 'First distance' εὐθεῖα πρώτα, 'first area' χωρίον πρῶτον bounded by first revolution and first distance, 'first circle' κύκλος πρῶτος described with first distance as radius and origin as centre. Forward τὰ προαγούμενα and backward τὰ ἑπόμενα for directions relative to radius vector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the dynamical description and the Greek technical terms for successive revolutions, distances, areas and radii used in spiral constructions—useful when translating kinetic/parametric constructions and area enumerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangent vocabulary and verb distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: To touch (meet) generally ἅπτομαι (but not necessarily 'touch'); to touch a curve or surface specifically ἐφάπτεσθαι or ἐπιψαύειν (with gen.). A tangent is ἐφαπτομένη or ἐπιψαύουσα (sc. εὐθεῖα). Tangent plane ἐπίπεδον (ἐπιψαύοντα ἐπίπεδα). Point of contact ἡ ἁφή. Different verbs distinguish 'meet', 'touch without cutting', 'touch at one point'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies subtle differences between Greek verbs used for tangency and contact vs. mere meeting; important to preserve mathematical meaning (e.g., 'meets' vs. 'touches') in translation and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructions: verbs and imperative passive usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety of Greek verbs for drawing/producing lines: ἀγω and compounds διάγω, κατάγω, προσάγω; προσβάλλω, προσπίπτω, ἐκβάλλω, ἐκπίπτω, πρόσκειμαι. Constructions are often expressed by the perfect imperative passive (γεγονέτω, ἔστω, κείσθω) or aorist imperative passive; many specimen imperatives: κείσθω τῷ Δ ἴσον τὸ BY; διήχθω τις εἰς αὐτὸν εὐθεῖα; ἐπεζεύχθω (let it be joined); ἐκβεβλήσθωσαν (let them be produced); ἐκκείσθω κύκλος (let a circle be set out).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the lexicon and grammatical forms typically used in classical geometric constructions, with many example phrases—critical for translating prescriptions like 'let X be drawn', and for recognizing passive imperatives in source texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructions: passive 'let it be conceived' and active forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Another method is the passive imperative of νοέω (νοείσθω) 'let it be conceived' (e.g., νοείσθωσαν εὐθεῖαι), sometimes participles omit 'drawn'. Active forms occur with ἐὰν + subjunctive, participles, or first-person (λαμβάνω, ἔλαβον). The genitive of passive participle used absolutely (εὑρεθέντος δή).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains alternative idioms (conceptual suppositions vs. explicit constructions) used by Archimedes and other authors. Important for recognizing hypothetical constructions vs. performed constructions and for rendering them properly in English.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructions: other verbs (make similar, experiment, cut unevenly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other verbs: to make a figure similar δμοιώσαι (δημοιώσαι?), to find experimentally ὀργανικῶς λαβεῖν, to cut into unequal parts εἰς ἄνισα τέμνειν.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists less common verbs that appear in geometric contexts; useful for particular constructions or methodological remarks in proofs (e.g., experimental finding, cutting unequally).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations — Addition and sums vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: To add προστίθημι; passive πρόσκειμαι used; being added together συντίθεσθαι; sums expressed by συναμφότερος (sum of BA, AA is συναμφότερος ἡ BAA), or more generally σύν/μετά for 'plus'. Phrasings for sums of areas/lines/circles (σύγκειται ἐκ used for 'is equal to the sum of').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives precise Greek verbs, participles and noun-phrases for addition and sum formation as used in geometrical algebraic-like discourse—useful for rendering arithmetic/combinatorial sentences in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations — Subtraction and differences vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: To subtract ἀφαιρεῖν ἀπό; remainder described by λοιπός (the remaining); difference/excess ὑπεροχή or ὑπεροχά (the excess by which one magnitude exceeds another), also ὑπερέχειν as verb and λείπεται for opposite. Examples: κοινὸν ἀφῃρήσθω τὸ χωρίον (let common area be subtracted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the Greek verbs and nouns used to indicate subtraction, remainders and excesses and sample constructions. Important for correctly translating steps that remove common parts or describe excesses in comparisons.
